plan: Two informative essays weighted toward Production of Writing: CLD-P-ACT-E-000075 on the WPA Pack Horse Library Project in eastern Kentucky (1935-1943; donated material, scrapbooks) and CLD-P-ACT-E-000076 on the Frisbee (Frisbie Pie Company story, Morrison and Franscioni 1948, Pluto Platter sold to Wham-O 1957, renamed 1958, Headrick's ridges, Ultimate 1968 at Columbia High School, disc golf baskets). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus E072-19 (revision 2) on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000074. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Libraries on Horseback
From Pie Tins to Playing Fields
passages.text:
[1] According to a popular story, college students in New England once entertained themselves by tossing empty pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut. [2] The tins flew surprisingly well, but they {{1|were made of metal, they}} could hurt anyone who failed to catch one.

[3] In 1948, Walter Frederick Morrison and his business partner, Warren Franscioni, produced a flying disc made of plastic{{2|, which was lighter and safer to catch than a pie tin.}} [4] Morrison kept refining the design, and in 1957 he sold the rights to his newest version{{3|, the Pluto Platter,}} to Wham-O, a California toy company. [5] A year later, {{4|the company, which was Wham-O, decided to rename the disc with a new name, calling it}} the Frisbee. [6] One of the company's founders had heard about the pie-tin game and borrowed the name, {{5|alternating}} its spelling slightly. [7] Sales soon soared.

[8] {{6|As a result,}} the early disc still wobbled in flight and was hard to throw accurately. [9] In the 1960s, Ed Headrick, a designer at Wham-O, added a series of raised ridges near the edge of the disc's top surface. [10] The ridges {{7|steadies}} the disc in flight, making long, accurate throws possible for players of {{8|all skill level's}}.

[11] {{9|Wham-O also sold other popular toys, such as the hula hoop.}} [12] In 1968, a group of students at Columbia High School in Maplewood, New Jersey, invented Ultimate, a team sport {{10|in which}} players may not run while holding the disc. [13] A few years later, Headrick helped launch disc golf, in which players throw discs toward a series of targets, and he designed the {{11|things}} still used as targets on many courses. [14] {{12|Today, Wham-O sells many other toys as well.}}

passages.title: A Bear in a Ranger's Hat

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: having literacy rates among the lowest
choices.D: the literacy rates of it being among the lowest

candidates.evidence: had no public libraries, few paved roads, and
candidates.explanation: The series lists things the region had: "no public libraries," "few paved roads," and "literacy rates among the lowest."

A.rationale: A full clause breaks the series of noun phrases ("no public libraries, few paved roads").

B.rationale: "Having" turns the last item into a verb phrase that does not match the others.

D.rationale: This is wordy and does not match the noun phrases in the series.

hints: What form do the first two items in the series take?

strategy.explanation: Compare the last item with the first two.

candidates.remember: Items in a series should share the same grammatical form.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: a program to bring books to these isolated communities
candidates.explanation: The subject "the Works Progress Administration" needs a main verb; "began funding" supplies one.

A.rationale: "Beginning to fund" is not a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

B.rationale: "Having begun" is not a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

D.rationale: "Which" turns the verb into part of a clause, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject of the sentence, and what is its verb?

strategy.explanation: Skip the phrase between the commas and find the verb.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a subject and a main verb.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Horses were also widely used on Kentucky farms for plowing fields and hauling timber.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the program chose to hire local women as librarians.
choices.B: Yes, because it shows that horses were the only practical way to travel in the region.
choices.C: No, because it shifts from the library program to a general fact about farm work.
choices.D: No, because it contradicts the claim that the librarians rode horses or mules.

candidates.evidence: became known as pack horse librarians
candidates.explanation: The paragraph introduces the library program and its workers; farm uses of horses are a digression.

A.rationale: The sentence says nothing about hiring women.

B.rationale: The sentence describes farm uses of horses, not travel.

D.rationale: The sentence does not contradict the essay; it is simply off topic.

hints: What is the paragraph about?

strategy.explanation: Compare the new sentence with the paragraph's focus.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: mountain trails that rose and fell steeply
choices.C: mountain trails, which were in the mountains

candidates.evidence: following creek beds and steep
candidates.explanation: "Steep mountain trails" says everything needed; the added clauses repeat ideas already given.

A.rationale: "Mountain trails" already says the trails were in the mountains, so "that went up and down the mountains" repeats it.

B.rationale: "Steep" already says the trails rose and fell sharply.

hints: Which words repeat an idea the sentence already expresses?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without the underlined portion.

candidates.remember: Cut words that repeat what the sentence already says.

candidates.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it describes the conditions that make the librarians' reliability notable.
choices.B: Kept, because it explains why the program chose mules rather than horses for the most difficult routes.
choices.C: Deleted, because it repeats information about the trails that was already given in the previous sentence.
choices.D: Deleted, because it shifts the focus of the paragraph from the librarians to the region's weather.

candidates.evidence: the librarians rarely missed a scheduled visit
candidates.explanation: The icy and muddy trails explain why rarely missing a visit was impressive; "Still" in the next sentence depends on them.

B.rationale: The sentence says nothing about choosing mules over horses.

C.rationale: The previous sentence describes the route, not the seasonal conditions.

D.rationale: The weather detail supports the point about the librarians' reliability.

hints: What does the next sentence's opening word contrast with?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentences before and after.

candidates.remember: Keep a sentence that the next sentence depends on.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: the librarians rarely missed a scheduled visit
candidates.explanation: The librarians kept their schedule despite the hard conditions, so the contrast word "Still" fits.

B.rationale: The hard conditions would not cause the librarians to keep their schedule.

C.rationale: Rarely missing a visit is not similar to icy and muddy trails.

D.rationale: Keeping the schedule is not an example of the trail conditions.

hints: How does keeping the schedule relate to the icy, muddy trails?

strategy.explanation: Name the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Choose the transition that matches the logical relationship.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: children often ran down the hollows to meet the riders
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to "the riders," which is plural, so "their" is needed.

A.rationale: "Its" is singular, but it refers to the plural "riders."

C.rationale: "His or her" is singular, but "riders" is plural.

D.rationale: "One's" does not refer to the riders.

hints: What noun does the pronoun refer to, and is it singular or plural?

strategy.explanation: Find the antecedent.

candidates.remember: A pronoun must agree in number with its antecedent.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: libraries, schools, and private citizens from across the country
candidates.explanation: "By libraries, schools, and private citizens" completes "was donated," so no punctuation should separate them.

A.rationale: No comma belongs between "donated" and "by," which completes the verb phrase.

B.rationale: No comma belongs between the parts of the verb.

D.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate a verb from the phrase that completes it.

hints: Is there any reason to pause between the verb and the phrase that follows it?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without any added punctuation.

candidates.remember: Do not separate a verb from the phrase that completes it.

candidates.stem: Which choice provides the most specific description of what the scrapbooks contained?

choices.B: of recipes, quilt patterns, and short stories
choices.C: of many different kinds of printed material
choices.D: of whatever the librarians had decided to save

candidates.evidence: cut out usable pages and pasted them into scrapbooks
candidates.explanation: Only this choice names specific contents of the scrapbooks.

A.rationale: "Various things" gives no specific information.

C.rationale: This is still general and names no specific contents.

D.rationale: This does not say what was saved.

hints: Which choice names actual items?

strategy.explanation: Compare how specific each choice is.

candidates.remember: When asked for specific detail, choose concrete nouns.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: were totally loved by all the people
choices.C: went over really big with everybody

candidates.evidence: These homemade collections
candidates.explanation: The essay is written in a formal, informative style; "proved especially popular with families" matches it.

A.rationale: "A huge hit with the folks" is too informal for the essay.

B.rationale: "Totally loved" is too informal for the essay.

C.rationale: "Went over really big" is too informal for the essay.

hints: Which choice sounds like the rest of the essay?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate slang and casual phrases.

candidates.remember: Match the tone of the essay.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: The program ended in 1943
candidates.explanation: The plural subject "demands" and the past event in 1943 call for the simple past "drew."

A.rationale: "Was" is singular, but the subject "demands" is plural.

B.rationale: The present tense does not fit an event in 1943.

D.rationale: The present perfect does not fit a completed event in 1943.

hints: What is the subject of the verb, and when did the event happen?

strategy.explanation: Skip the prepositional phrase to find the subject.

candidates.remember: A verb must agree with its subject and fit the time frame.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by connecting to the situation described in the first sentence?

choices.B: In a region that had once had almost no libraries, reading had become part of everyday life.
choices.C: The Works Progress Administration also funded the construction of roads, bridges, and schools.
choices.D: Many of the librarians later found other jobs during the war years in their communities.

candidates.evidence: much of eastern Kentucky had no public libraries
candidates.explanation: The essay opens with a region lacking libraries; this choice shows how the program changed that.

A.rationale: The horses' sturdiness does not connect to the lack of libraries described at the start.

C.rationale: This shifts to other WPA projects.

D.rationale: This does not return to the situation in the first sentence.

hints: What problem does the first sentence describe?

strategy.explanation: Reread the first sentence before choosing.

candidates.remember: A strong conclusion often returns to the opening idea.

candidates.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay:
Some families even contributed recipes of their own to these scrapbooks.
The sentence would most logically be placed after:
candidates.evidence: pasted them into scrapbooks
candidates.explanation: "These scrapbooks" refers to the scrapbooks introduced in sentence 10.

A.rationale: The scrapbooks have not been mentioned yet.

B.rationale: Sentence 6 is about the librarians' schedule, not scrapbooks.

D.rationale: Sentence 13 summarizes the program; "these scrapbooks" would have no nearby reference.

hints: What does "these scrapbooks" refer to?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence the new one depends on.

candidates.remember: Place a sentence right after the idea it develops.

candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to describe a government program created to meet a specific need in one region. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains how a federal program brought books to isolated communities in Kentucky.
choices.B: Yes, because it compares the pack horse program with library programs that operated in several other states.
choices.C: No, because it focuses mainly on the hardships of travel in the mountains of Kentucky.
choices.D: No, because it never explains why the pack horse library program came to an end.

candidates.evidence: a program to bring books to these isolated communities
candidates.explanation: The essay describes the region's lack of libraries and the WPA program that met that need.

B.rationale: The essay makes no such comparison.

C.rationale: Travel conditions are one paragraph; the essay is about the program.

D.rationale: The essay says the program ended as wartime demands drew money and workers elsewhere.

hints: What need does the essay describe, and what met it?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the stated purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.D: were made of metal; and they

candidates.evidence: could hurt anyone who failed to catch one
candidates.explanation: "And" joins the two verbs "were made" and "could hurt," which share the subject "they."

A.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: A semicolon should not be followed by "and" in this sentence.

hints: Can the two parts share one subject?

strategy.explanation: Find where the second clause begins.

candidates.remember: Avoid joining two independent clauses with only a comma.

candidates.stem: If the writer were to delete the underlined portion (ending the sentence with a period), the essay would primarily lose:

choices.A: a detail showing that Morrison had once worked for the Frisbie Pie Company.
choices.B: a comparison between Morrison's plastic disc and the later Frisbee models that Wham-O made.
choices.C: evidence that Morrison's plastic disc quickly outsold the metal pie tins.
choices.D: an explanation of how the new disc solved the problem described in the preceding sentence.

candidates.evidence: could hurt anyone who failed to catch one
candidates.explanation: Sentence 2 says metal tins could hurt people; the phrase explains that the plastic disc was lighter and safer.

A.rationale: The phrase says nothing about Morrison's work history.

B.rationale: The phrase compares the disc with pie tins, not later models.

C.rationale: The phrase says nothing about sales.

hints: What problem does the sentence before this one describe?

strategy.explanation: Connect the phrase to the previous sentence.

candidates.remember: Ask what job a phrase does before deciding what would be lost.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: to Wham-O, a California toy company
candidates.explanation: "The Pluto Platter" renames "his newest version," so it is set off by a pair of commas.

B.rationale: An appositive in the middle of a sentence needs a comma on both sides.

C.rationale: An appositive in the middle of a sentence needs a comma on both sides.

D.rationale: A semicolon cannot set off an appositive.

hints: Could the phrase be removed without breaking the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check that the commas come in a matched pair.

candidates.remember: Set off a nonessential appositive with matching commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: the company, Wham-O, made the decision to rename the disc by calling it
choices.D: Wham-O, the company, renamed the disc and gave it the new name of

candidates.evidence: A year later,
candidates.explanation: "The company renamed the disc the Frisbee" says the idea clearly with no repetition.

A.rationale: The company is already identified, and "rename" and "with a new name" repeat each other.

B.rationale: This still includes needless words and repeats the company's name.

D.rationale: "Renamed" and "gave it the new name" repeat each other.

hints: Which words repeat information the reader already has?

strategy.explanation: Choose the shortest version that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: Cut repeated or unnecessary words.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: borrowed the name
candidates.explanation: The founder changed the spelling slightly, so "altering" is the correct word.

A.rationale: "Alternating" means switching back and forth, which does not fit.

C.rationale: "Altared" is not a word; "altar" is a noun.

D.rationale: "Alterating" is not a standard English word.

hints: What did the founder do to the spelling of the name?

strategy.explanation: Check each word's meaning in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Watch for words that look alike but mean different things.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Sales soon soared.
candidates.explanation: The disc sold well despite a flaw, so a contrast transition fits.

A.rationale: The wobbling was not caused by the soaring sales.

B.rationale: The wobbling is not an example of the soaring sales.

D.rationale: The wobbling is not similar to soaring sales; it is a problem despite them.

hints: How does a flaw in the disc relate to its strong sales?

strategy.explanation: Name the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Choose the transition that matches the logical relationship.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: added a series of raised ridges
candidates.explanation: The plural subject "ridges" and the past-tense narration call for "steadied."

A.rationale: "Steadies" is singular and present, but the subject "ridges" is plural and the essay is in the past tense.

C.rationale: "Has" is singular, but the subject "ridges" is plural.

D.rationale: "Steadying" is not a main verb, so the sentence becomes a fragment.

hints: What is the subject, and what tense is the paragraph in?

strategy.explanation: Check the verbs in nearby sentences.

candidates.remember: Keep verbs consistent with their subjects and with the essay's tense.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: making long, accurate throws possible for players
candidates.explanation: "Levels" is a simple plural with no possession, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.rationale: The apostrophe makes a possessive, but nothing belongs to the level.

B.rationale: The plural possessive is wrong because nothing belongs to the levels.

C.rationale: This changes the meaning and is not idiomatic.

hints: Does anything belong to the skill level?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether the word is plural, possessive, or both.

candidates.remember: Plural nouns that show no possession take no apostrophe.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively introduces the main topic of this paragraph?

choices.A: These steadier throws soon made entirely new games possible.
choices.C: Ultimate is sometimes described as a mix of soccer and football.
choices.D: Some people still prefer to throw the disc simply for fun.

candidates.evidence: invented Ultimate, a team sport
candidates.explanation: The paragraph describes Ultimate and disc golf; this choice links the accurate throws from the previous paragraph to the new games.

B.rationale: The paragraph is about new sports, not other Wham-O toys.

C.rationale: This mentions only one of the paragraph's two sports and ignores the link to Headrick's ridges.

D.rationale: This does not introduce the sports discussed in the paragraph.

hints: What do the sentences in this paragraph describe?

strategy.explanation: Read the whole paragraph before choosing.

candidates.remember: A topic sentence should cover the whole paragraph and link it to the one before.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: players may not run while holding the disc
candidates.explanation: "In which" correctly introduces a clause that describes what happens in the sport.

B.rationale: Without "in," "which" leaves the clause ungrammatical; the players do not hold the sport itself.

C.rationale: "In that" means "because" and does not describe the sport.

D.rationale: "Where in" is not idiomatic.

hints: Does the clause describe what happens within the sport?

strategy.explanation: Read each choice in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Use "in which" to describe what happens within something.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: still used as targets on many courses
candidates.explanation: Only this choice says what the targets actually are.

A.rationale: "Things" is vague.

B.rationale: This is still vague.

C.rationale: This does not say what the targets are.

hints: Which choice tells the reader what the targets look like?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate vague choices.

candidates.remember: Prefer precise words to vague ones.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by connecting the disc's present-day use to its origins?

choices.B: Today, many college students still enjoy playing catch on their campus lawns during free time between classes.
choices.C: Today, both sports are played worldwide, and a toy inspired by pie tins has become serious athletic gear.
choices.D: Today, a number of companies besides Wham-O manufacture flying discs for players around the world.

candidates.evidence: tossing empty pie tins
candidates.explanation: Only this choice ties the disc's role in modern sports back to the pie tins described at the start.

A.rationale: This mentions Wham-O but not the disc's origins or its use in sports.

B.rationale: This does not mention the disc's use in sports or its pie-tin origins.

D.rationale: This does not connect the disc to its origins.

hints: How does the essay begin?

strategy.explanation: Reread the first sentence before choosing.

candidates.remember: A strong conclusion often returns to the opening idea.

candidates.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay:
The name stuck, even though the pie company itself had closed by then.
The sentence would most logically be placed after:
candidates.evidence: borrowed the name
candidates.explanation: Sentence 6 explains that the founder borrowed the pie company's name; the new sentence follows directly from it.

A.rationale: The disc has not been named the Frisbee yet.

B.rationale: "Pluto Platter" is not the name that stuck, and the pie company's name has not been borrowed yet.

D.rationale: Sentence 9 is about Headrick's ridges, not the name.

hints: Which sentence describes borrowing the pie company's name?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence the new one depends on.

candidates.remember: Place a sentence right after the idea it develops.

candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how a single inventor created a popular toy. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains how Morrison invented the Frisbee on his own in 1948.
choices.B: Yes, because it focuses on Ed Headrick's role in designing the modern disc.
choices.C: No, because it focuses mainly on the rules of Ultimate and disc golf.
choices.D: No, because it shows that several people contributed to the disc's development.

candidates.evidence: Walter Frederick Morrison and his business partner, Warren Franscioni
candidates.explanation: The essay credits several people, so it does not show a single inventor.

A.rationale: The essay credits Morrison, Franscioni, Wham-O's founders, and Headrick.

B.rationale: Headrick is one of several contributors.

C.rationale: The sports are mentioned briefly; the rules are not the focus.

hints: How many people does the essay credit?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the stated purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

candidates.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay:
Its message was simple: before leaving a campsite, make sure the fire is completely out.
The sentence would most logically be placed after:
candidates.evidence: The first poster showed the bear pouring a bucket of water on a campfire
candidates.explanation: "Its message" refers to the first poster, which sentence 3 describes; the campfire image matches the message about putting out fires.

A.rationale: The poster has not been introduced yet, so "Its message" would have no clear reference.

C.rationale: This sentence is about the rescued cub, not a poster.

D.rationale: "Its" would refer to the campaign's 2001 slogan, and the message about campsites would be out of place.

hints: What does "Its" refer to?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence the new one depends on.

candidates.remember: Place a sentence right after the idea it develops.
